The Seven Wonders of the Jagannath Temple

Temple Stories

The Seven Wonders of the Jagannath Temple

The Mysteries of Puri

In everyday English — the temple's own telling

Stories by Eku

How to Read · · BEFORE WE BEGIN

Read it aloud. This story is made to be told — slowly, as if you are sitting with everyone at home and telling it to them.

This book is the companion of two books. In the first book — Jagannath of Puri — we heard how King Indradyumna searched for Nilamadhava, how the Daru Brahma came from the sea, how the old carpenter carved the unfinished forms, and how Brahma consecrated them. In the second book — Jagannath's Living Traditions — we saw what happens with those forms today, every year, and every few years — the bath, the chariot festival, the new body, and the daily prasad. None of that story is repeated here. Here we will hear seven wonders told about the temple — the things every devotee who goes to Puri hears, and tells everyone when they come home.

Let one thing be clear from the start. These seven things are not scripture — they are the temple's own story, told by the devotees. Some things can really be seen — like the flag being changed every evening. Some things are folk lore — like the wheel seeming to face you from every direction. And some things may have an ordinary meaning too — like the shadow falling on the temple's own courtyard. So every part carries its own separate note — it tells you what can be seen, what is folk lore, and what the ordinary meaning is. Nothing is mixed into the main story.

The yellow boxes are people speaking in their own words — change your voice a little. (Purple cues) tell you where to pause or whisper — do not read them aloud. At the end of every part, the green box — Pause and think. Stop there, ask questions, let the listener speak.

So come — standing on Puri's grand road, looking toward the Lion Gate, let us hear the seven wonders — one by one.

The Seven Wonders at a Glance · · THE SEVEN WONDERS AT A GLANCE

Seven things are told about the temple of Puri more than any others. Hear them together first — then the full story of each one will come.

  • 1 · The flag against the wind — the temple flag flies in the opposite direction of the wind, and every day a servitor climbs the 214-foot tower without a rope to change it.
  • 2 · The blue wheel — the Nilachakra of eight metals on the tower, which seems to face you no matter where in Puri you look from.
  • 3 · The tower without a shadow — at no time of day is the main tower's shadow seen.
  • 4 · The empty sky — no bird flies over the tower, and no aeroplane passes above it.
  • 5 · The sea's voice at the Lion Gate — outside the gate you hear the waves of the sea; step inside, and the sound stops.
  • 6 · The upside-down kitchen — in the temple kitchen, earthen pots are stacked one above another, and the food in the topmost pot cooks first.
  • 7 · The food that never runs out — the Mahaprasad feeds thousands and never runs out.

One thing is the same in all seven — every one of them happens above the temple, or at its gate, or in its kitchen. As if the temple itself is saying — 'Come, look, think.'

1 · The Flag Against the Wind · · THE FLAG AGAINST THE WIND

Whoever comes to Puri sees one thing first — the red flag flying at the very top of the temple. It is called the Patitapavana Bana — 'the flag that makes the fallen pure'. This flag is tied above the Nilachakra — and people say it flies in the opposite direction of the wind.

Down on the street the trees may bend one way — the flag will be flying the other way. The flags below may fly in one direction — the flag above flies in the opposite direction. The people of Puri say — no matter which way the wind blows, Jagannath's flag flies in its own direction.

But the real wonder is not the direction of the flag — the real wonder is that this flag is changed every day. Every evening, between about four and six o'clock, the Chunara sevaks — also called the Garuda sevaks — climb the tower. Two hundred and fourteen feet — without a rope, without a ladder, barefoot, on the smooth stone wall. They take down the old flag, put up the new one, and climb slowly back down. As told in Jagannath's Living Traditions, this service has gone on for centuries without a break — and thousands of people gather in the temple courtyard in the evening to watch the flag being changed.

They say, if the flag is not changed even for a single day, the temple will have to stay closed for eighteen years. So the sevaks of the Chunara families never give up this service — generation after generation.

Devotees say — "As soon as you come to Puri, the flag is seen from far away — that itself is darshan."

(Pause here and look upward — as if you are watching the flag.)

The flag and the wind — what can be seen, what is folk lore

That the flag is changed every day can be seen: the Chunara sevaks climb the tower barefoot without a rope every evening, roughly between four and six o'clock, and change the Patitapavana Bana. This rite is recorded in the temple administration's accounts and in many articles. That the flag flies in the opposite direction of the wind is what the devotees say — the wind below and the wind above are not the same; eddies at height and the changing sea breeze can make the flag seem to fly in the opposite direction. 'If it is missed for one day, the temple stays closed for eighteen years' is also what tradition says; no written rule for it was found.

Pause and think — The flag is new every day — but the temple is the same old one. Does doing something new every day keep an old thing alive — like a new sun every morning? And the sevak who climbs without a rope — is trust also a kind of rope?

2 · The Blue Wheel · · THE BLUE WHEEL

At the very top of the tower, below the flag, there is a great blue wheel — the Nilachakra. It is the form of Lord Vishnu's Sudarshan Chakra — and they say it is made of eight metals — ashtadhatu: gold, silver, copper, iron, tin, lead, zinc and mercury.

Two things are said about the Nilachakra. The first — it is so big and heavy that how it was lifted to the top of the tower centuries ago, without cranes and without machines, is still a wonder today. The second — no matter where in Puri you look from, the wheel seems to face only you. Look from the east, and it faces you; look from the west, and it faces you; look from the north, and still it faces you. As if the wheel is watching everyone.

The Nilachakra is also told of in Jagannath's Living Traditions — there it is flagged as folk lore in its own note. Here is the full telling — the wheel has eight spokes toward the eight directions, and its round shape looks the same from every direction. So no matter where you look from, it seems to face you.

They say the Nilachakra casts no shadow either — and that in the salty sea air for hundreds of years it neither rusts nor gathers dust.

The people of Puri say — "Look at the wheel from wherever you like, it is looking at you — as if the Lord's gaze is on everyone."

The Nilachakra — what can be seen, what is folk lore

The Nilachakra is made of ashtadhatu — an alloy of eight metals — as recorded in the temple's accounts. It is about three and a half metres across and has eight spokes. 'The wheel faces you from every direction' is folk lore: the wheel is round and symmetrical, so from every direction it looks as if it faces you. How the wheel was lifted up without cranes — no firm source was found; one popular tale says it was placed there by the divine architect Vishwakarma. The wheel's weight also varies wildly between accounts — from about 150 kg to 2,000 kg — so no weight is given in the main story.

Pause and think — The wheel is round — it has no front and no back. Is the Lord like that too — before everyone, in every direction, the same? And the thing that was lifted up centuries ago without machines — did the people of old also have a craft we have forgotten?

3 · The Tower Without a Shadow · · THE TOWER WITHOUT A SHADOW

The temple of Puri is very tall — 214 feet, about 65 metres. Such a tall stone tower, in the sunlight — its shadow should fall far away. But the people of Puri say — the main tower's shadow is never seen — not in the morning, not at noon, not in the evening, at no time of day.

In the morning the sun rises in the east — the shadow should fall to the west. At noon the sun is overhead — the shadow should fall below. In the evening the sun sets in the west — the shadow should fall to the east. But people say — the tower's shadow is seen nowhere. As if the tower stands in the sunlight, but the sunlight never touches it.

Every traveller who comes to Puri hears this — and stands in the temple courtyard and looks for themselves. The tower is tall, the sun is strong — and still no shadow.

Travellers ask — "Such a tall tower, and no shadow? How can that be?" — and the people of Puri smile and say — "That is Jagannath's wonder."

The shadow — what can be seen, what the ordinary meaning is

'The tower's shadow is never seen' is what the devotees say; no measured, written proof of the shadow's absence was found. The ordinary meaning may be this: the tower's shadow falls on the temple's own great complex — the Jagamohana, the Natamandapa, the Bhogamandapa and the high walls — so it is not seen separately on the ground. The tall, curving shape of the Kalinga style helps too. This is said here so that the ordinary meaning stands beside the wonder-tale.

Pause and think — Everything casts a shadow — a tree, a house, even us. If something casts no shadow — does it become greater than the sunlight? And not seeing a shadow — is that also a kind of darshan?

4 · The Empty Sky · · THE EMPTY SKY

Puri is on the shore of the sea — and by the sea there are many birds — crows, pigeons, sea eagles. They sit on every roof, on the tower of every temple. But the people of Puri say — no bird flies over the Jagannath temple's tower — and no aeroplane passes above it either.

Birds fly around the temple — in the courtyard, on the streets, over the sea. But the sky directly above the tower stays empty — as if some invisible line is drawn there, which no one crosses.

People say — this place belongs to the Lord, so even the birds respectfully do not fly over it. Some people call it a no-fly zone — as if the temple has its own courtyard even in the sky.

Devotees say — "Even the birds know — do not fly over it, come and see it from the front."

Birds and aeroplanes — what can be seen, what is folk lore

'No bird or aeroplane passes over the tower' is what the devotees say. There is no official no-fly zone above the temple — India's civil aviation authorities have declared no such zone. And one more thing: on 13 April 2025 an eagle — which people call the Shankha Chila — was seen flying above the temple, carrying a flag bearing the Nilachakra in its claws. So 'no bird ever flies above' is not fully true; it is the temple's folk lore, not a rule.

Pause and think — Birds are the kings of the sky — they can fly anywhere. If they too fly around some place — is that place really different? And if one eagle did fly above — does the wonder become smaller, or bigger?

5 · The Sea's Voice at the Lion Gate · · THE SEA'S VOICE AT THE LION GATE

The temple of Puri is not far from the sea — the Mahodadhi, the great sea, is only a short distance from the temple. The sound of the sea's waves is heard everywhere on the streets of Puri — roaring, without stopping.

But they say — the moment you step inside through the temple's main gate — the Singhadwar, the Lion Gate — the sound of the sea stops. Outside the gate, the roar of the waves — inside the gate, silence. Step outside, and the sound comes back at once. As if the gate itself stops the sound.

Every devotee who goes to Puri tries this for themselves — standing at the gate, one step outside, one step inside. Outside, noise; inside, silence. People say — to hear the Lord's voice inside the temple, you have to leave the sea's voice outside.

Devotees say — "Outside the gate the sea roars — inside, Jagannath smiles."

(Lower your voice here — as if you are standing inside the temple.)

The sea's voice — the checked telling, and the reel's opposite version

The main story carries the telling that was checked: outside the gate the sea's voice is heard; step inside, and it stops — this is written the same way in many articles. The reel this book began from told it the opposite way in its own narration — sound inside, silence outside — but that does not match the checked accounts, so it is not used in the main story. The ordinary meaning may be this: the temple's high walls — the Meghanada Pacheri — and the shape of the halls inside block the sea's sound, so inside it feels silent.

Pause and think — The sea's voice stops at the gate — as if the temple is saying, 'Now be quiet.' Is silence also a part of darshan — like staying quiet inside the temple? And outside noise, inside silence — is the gate itself the line between two worlds?

6 · The Upside-Down Kitchen · · THE UPSIDE-DOWN KITCHEN

Now let us come down from the tower into the kitchen — the Rosaghara, called the largest temple kitchen in the world. There are 752 earthen hearths there — and hundreds of cooks — the Suaras — who have done the same work for generations. As told in Jagannath's Living Traditions, the food is cooked in earthen pots over a wood fire — without onion or garlic, only with native vegetables.

The wonder of the kitchen is this — on one hearth the earthen pots are stacked one above another — seven pots, one on top of another, over the fire. And they say — the food in the topmost pot cooks first — then the one below it, then the one below that — and the bottommost pot, which is closest to the fire, cooks last of all.

Think of it — the fire is below, but the food above cooks first. It is upside down — as if the fire is burning from above, not from below. The cooks say — this happens every day, without fail, for hundreds of years.

The cooks say — "The topmost pot cooks first — because Jagannath's grace comes from above."

About the number of pots

The earthen pots are stacked one above another on one hearth — in most accounts seven pots, in some nine. As told in Jagannath's Living Traditions too, both counts are found — so seven is written here, because that is the count found most often.

Why the topmost pot cooks first

'The topmost pot cooks first' is what the kitchen says, recorded in many articles. The ordinary meaning may be this: the earthen pots are unglazed — steam rises through them and gathers in the topmost pot, cooking it first. But no measured scientific proof of this was found — so here it stands as folk lore, not as proven fact.

Pause and think — The fire is below, the food above cooks first — upside down! Can being upside down also be right — like a younger brother growing up first sometimes? And what happens every day in the kitchen — is that itself the wonder, happening again and again?

7 · The Food That Never Runs Out · · THE FOOD THAT NEVER RUNS OUT

From the kitchen the food comes out — and becomes Mahaprasad. First the offering is made to Jagannath, then it is taken before Goddess Vimala — then it becomes Mahaprasad. Then it is found in the Ananda Bazaar — the open market inside the temple, where everyone sits together and eats.

And here is the seventh wonder — they say, the Mahaprasad never runs out. Whether thousands come or lakhs — everyone gets food, and it neither falls short nor is left over. As if the kitchen knows how many people will come today — and cooks exactly that much.

Every day thousands of people come — on festivals, lakhs. In the kitchen the Chhapan Bhog — fifty-six kinds of dishes — are made. And they say, whether two thousand come or twenty thousand — the prasad is always exactly right. No one goes back hungry, and no food is thrown away.

Devotees say — "Here no one is big, no one is small — everyone is of the same plate."

The Mahaprasad — what can be seen, what is folk lore

That the Mahaprasad feeds thousands of people every day can be seen: hundreds of cooks in the Rosaghara, 752 hearths and the Chhapan Bhog are made every day, and in the Ananda Bazaar everyone gets prasad. 'The prasad never falls short, and is never left over' is what the devotees say. The ordinary meaning is this: the kitchen cooks in very large quantities and raises or lowers the quantity according to the crowd — more on festivals, less on ordinary days — so everyone gets prasad. 'Never running out' is the poetic form of that, not a claim of accounts.

Pause and think — Food shared does not run out — does it grow? Is sharing also a kind of cooking — like love, which does not lessen when shared? And everyone sitting together to eat — rich and poor, big and small — does food also teach equality?

All Seven Together · · ALL SEVEN TOGETHER

So the seven wonders have been heard — the flag, the wheel, the shadow, the sky, the sea's voice, the upside-down kitchen, and the food that never runs out. Now look at them together — is there one thread running through them?

The first four wonders are above — the flag, the wheel, the shadow and the sky — around the tower. The fifth wonder is at the gate — the sea's voice at the Lion Gate. The last two wonders are inside — the kitchen and the prasad. As if the temple is saying — look up, stop at the gate, come inside — there is something everywhere.

And one more thing — not one of these seven is from scripture. They are all the temple's own story — told by the devotees, generation after generation. Scripture tells us who the Lord is; these wonders tell us how the devotees see the Lord — every day, from every direction, at every gate.

So do not take these seven as things to prove — take them as things to hear. Like a grandmother's story — whether it is true or not is a later question; first listen, think, and then go to Puri yourself and see.

Farewell · · FAREWELL

So this was the story of the seven wonders of the Puri temple — the flag that flies against the wind, the wheel that looks at everyone, the tower that casts no shadow, the sky that stays empty, the gate where the sea's voice stops, the kitchen where the topmost pot cooks first, and the prasad that never runs out.

The special thing about Puri is this — here the Lord does not only sit inside the temple. He comes out — onto the streets, onto the chariots, to his aunt's house. And the temple too is not only stone — every day it says something — through the flag, through the wheel, through the steam of the kitchen.

The next time you go to Puri, do not stop only at the temple's gate — look up at the flag, look at the wheel, stand at the gate and listen to the sea's voice — and sit in the Ananda Bazaar and eat the prasad.

Jai Jagannath!

Pause and think — Of these seven wonders, which did you like the most — the flag, the wheel, the shadow, the sky, the sea's voice, the upside-down kitchen — or the food that never runs out?

About this book

This book began from the Divine Stories Studio reel 'Puri Jagannath Mandir Ke 7 Chamatkar' (18 November 2026) — but the reel was only a pointer, never a source. Every telling was checked before it was written — and what could not be checked is told separately in its own note.

Sources · · SOURCES

Every telling in this book was checked before it was written — but this book is not scripture. Its main story is the living tradition of the Puri temple and the things the devotees say — and its sources are the same: the temple administration's accounts, articles written about the temple, and Puri's tradition. No palm-leaf manuscripts of the Puranas were seen — only the accounts written about them are the sources. Where accounts differ, that is told separately in its own note.

The earlier books

Jagannath of Puri (Temple Stories, first book) — King Indradyumna's search, the Daru Brahma, the old carpenter and the consecration; and Jagannath's Living Traditions (second book) — the bath, the chariot festival, the new body, the daily rite, the Mahaprasad, the temple today and the festivals. What this book says about the flag change, the Nilachakra, the Mahaprasad and the number of pots matches the second book — there is the full story, here is the wonder's own story.

The flag and the Chunara sevaks

The daily flag change, the Chunara (Garuda) sevaks climbing barefoot without a rope, the Patitapavana Bana, the time of about four to six o'clock — from the temple administration's accounts and articles written about Puri. The flag flying against the wind is what the devotees say; eddies at height and the sea breeze may be its ordinary meaning.

The Nilachakra

Ashtadhatu, eight spokes, a size of about three and a half metres, its place on the tower — from the temple's accounts. 'Seeming to face you from every direction' is folk lore; the wheel's round, symmetrical shape is its ordinary meaning. How the wheel was lifted up without cranes — no firm source was found.

The shadow, the birds and the aeroplanes

'The tower's shadow is never seen' and 'no bird or aeroplane passes over the tower' are the devotees' tellings, recorded in many articles about Puri. The ordinary meaning of the shadow is that it falls on the temple's own complex. About the birds: there is no official no-fly zone above the temple, and on 13 April 2025 an eagle was seen flying above the temple.

The sea's voice

'Sound outside the gate, silence inside' is written the same way in many articles. The reel's own narration told it the opposite way — that does not match the checked accounts, so it is not used in the main story. The walls and the halls may be its ordinary meaning.

The kitchen and the Mahaprasad

The Rosaghara, 752 hearths, hundreds of Suara cooks, the Chhapan Bhog, earthen pots, food without onion or garlic, Goddess Vimala and the Ananda Bazaar — from Puri's living tradition. The stack of seven pots (nine in some accounts) and the topmost pot cooking first are what the kitchen says; rising steam may be its ordinary meaning. 'The prasad never runs out' is what the devotees say; the kitchen's large, adjustable quantity is its ordinary meaning.

About the sources

There is no scriptural verse in this book — all seven wonders are the temple's folk lore. Where something could not be checked — how the wheel was lifted, the measurement of the shadow, the steam science of the kitchen — that is told separately in its own note. No deity form is shown in this book's pictures — only the temple, the flag, the wheel, the kitchen and the prasad.
